title: Desperate Spurs now have one task left this season: Survive in the Premier League
content:
Igor Tudor used “fragile” and “weak” in his post-match press conference. Inept, embarrassing and dreadful also work.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a team in Europe performing further below expectations than Tottenham Hotspur right now, but against Atletico Madrid on Tuesday night their floor somehow caved in again.

Tudor announced before the game that, in Tottenham’s desperate state, the Premier League would take precedence over the Champions League — the one competition where Spurs have not been totally calamitous this term. In publicly prioritising their domestic top-flight status — which is growing ever more perilous by the week — Tudor allowed himself to experiment away in the Spanish capital in the first leg of a European round-of-16 tie.

It could be the last time the boardroom let him cook.

Goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky was handed his first senior start since October in place of Guglielmo Vicario, a squad leader who has been playing well.

The 17 minutes Kinsky played before he was substituted are ones he won’t ever forget, confirming Vicario’s undisputed place in goal for the remainder of the season by default.

Sandwiched either side of an equally calamitous slip by defender Micky van de Ven, allowing Antoine Griezmann in for Atletico’s second, mishit passes by Kinsky led to two more easy early goals for the hosts — putting them far out of sight before Tottenham had the opportunity to even attempt to gain a foothold in the game.

A fourth was added soon after, on 22 minutes, with Pape Matar Sarr misdirecting his header towards Kinsky’s replacement Vicario, drawing a good save from the Italian, before Robin Le Normand converted the rebound.

“I’ve been coaching 15 years, I’ve never done this thing,” Tudor said in his post-match press conference, referring to substituting his goalkeeper. “It was necessary to preserve the guy, preserve the team. Incredible situation. Nothing to comment.

“It was, before the game, the right choice to do in the moment like we are. Pressure on Vicario. Another competition. Toni (Kinsky) is a very good goalkeeper. It was, for me, the right decision. After this, of course, it’s easy to say that it was not the right decision. So I explained to Toni, speaking after. He’s a right guy and good goalkeeper. Unfortunately (they) happened in this big game, these mistakes.”

According to former Manchester United and Denmark goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel, speaking on CBS Sports’ coverage of the match, it was a “moment that everybody in football will always remember every time they see or hear his name”. On TNT Sports’ UK broadcast, ex-Manchester City and England ‘keeper Joe Hart slammed Tudor’s lack of humanity in failing even to acknowledge Kinsky, who will turn 23 on Friday, as he left the pitch. Paul Robinson, who made 41 appearances in goal for England in his career, described it as “selfish” on BBC Radio 5 Live radio, claiming Tudor, presented as a specialist firefighter of a manager when he replaced the sacked Thomas Frank last month, was acting in “self-preservation”.

Aside from his employment, it’s hard to imagine Tudor wants to preserve anything from his dire 24-day, four-game spell as Tottenham coach to date. And when asked whether he is the right man for that job, one where he faces incessant questioning on his suitability for a role he has yet to show any promise in, he replied “no comment”. Words, he realises, count for precious little without substance.

Similar questions should be asked of those in the Spurs hierarchy who chose to appoint him.

Tudor has a reputation for improving faltering clubs in other big European leagues but it’s becoming increasingly apparent with every exasperated attempt to make sense of Tottenham’s “amazing” situation that he underestimated, or was undersold, the extent of the challenge awaiting in north London.

And misplacing long-term planning over the club’s pressing short-term needs no longer stands up to scrutiny. For that, sporting director Johan Lange, chief executive Vinai Venkatesham and the controlling Lewis family, headed by Nick Beucher and Vivienne Lewis, bear responsibility.

Had they acted after Mohammed Kudus sustained the hamstring injury he is yet to return from on January 4, perhaps fellow winger Ademola Lookman, who started for Atletico following a winter-window transfer from Atalanta of Italy and assisted their opening goal last night, might have been a Tottenham player in this tie instead. Had they identified the immediate, pressing need for a midfield playmaker with Dejan Kulusevski and James Maddison both yet to kick a ball in anger this season due to injury, perhaps Spurs would have been more successful in keeping possession.

This inaction, not just in January but over several transfer windows and key junctures, is more to blame for the collapse at the Metropolitano on Tuesday than the hapless Tudor’s choice to give Kinsky a go.

Yet it’s the Croatian who seems most likely to be heading for the exit door in the immediate future.

With Tottenham sitting 16th in the Premier League, just a point above the relegation zone with nine games left, the decision to stick or twist has rarely, if ever, had greater consequences. Tudor appears out of ideas at a time when Spurs need them most, but, given the circumstances, the list of possible alternatives is significantly shorter than the long line of injured players any replacement will have to make do without.

Also unavailable is Van de Ven, whose red card in the 3-1 defeat to Crystal Palace in the previous game rules him out of the trip to Liverpool on Sunday. He might be joined on the sidelines by defensive colleagues Joao Palhinha and Cristian Romero, who both finished last night’s tie off the pitch after an accidental clash of heads in second half stoppage time.

Losing Romero, who played his first game since earning a four-match ban for a second red card due to a late tackle on Manchester United midfielder Casemiro, for any more than the trip to Anfield would be a hammer blow, with a true relegation six-pointer coming up at home against Nottingham Forest the following Sunday.

Because if Tudor has got anything right as Tottenham coach, it’s that the 2025-26 Champions League didn’t matter for them before their 5-2 defeat on Tuesday, and it definitely doesn’t matter now.

Spurs have lost six games in a row for the first time in their history, and can hardly afford many more defeats in the next two months — but they’d surely accept another sound beating by Atletico in the second leg next Wednesday in return for a haul of four points from their next two Premier League matches in a heartbeat.
